titles.46: If I Could Turn Back Time

bank.q: Four episodes on a Tuesday evening, one after another, and she still calls it a coincidence rather than a habit of …

“We will release the whole series at once.” → They announced that they … the whole series at once.
Which reported question is correctly formed?
bank.a: He asked whether I had seen it.
d: He asked did I see it.
He asked have I seen it.
He asked me did I had seen it.

bank.q: You are reporting a claim you do not necessarily accept. Which verb signals that?
Which sentence reports the same fact without naming a source?
bank.a: The series is said to have cost forty million.
d: They say it cost forty million, whoever they are.
Somebody told me it cost forty million.
In my opinion it cost forty million.

bank.q: After six hours of questioning he … that he had taken the money.

Which reporting verb suggests the speaker was reluctant to say it?
Which sentence reports a disagreement neutrally?
bank.a: Both sides argued their case at some length.
d: Both sides refused to see sense.
Both sides claimed things that were untrue.
Both sides insisted on being difficult.

bank.q: A headline reads “Minister denies knowing of report”. What does the wording tell a careful reader?
bank.a: the claim is the minister's, and the paper is not endorsing it
d: the report definitely exists and was read
the paper has verified the denial

bank.a: The mine was allowed to reopen.
d: The mine had killed eight men.
Eight men were allowed to reopen.
The mine which was allowed to reopen.

bank.q: A long sentence is hard to follow. Which is usually the most useful first move?
bank.a: strip out the clauses between commas and dashes and read what is left
d: read it aloud twice at speed
look up every long word in it
start from the last clause and work backwards

bank.q: Which opening is most likely to keep a listener with a spoken story?
bank.a: You will not believe who was standing behind me.
d: I am going to tell you a story now.
Something happened to me last week.
This story is quite a long one.

bank.q: A story is described as “scannable”. That means it is …
bank.a: laid out so the eye can pick out the point quickly
d: short enough to read in a minute
written by more than one person

bank.a: each brain is subtracting a different assumed light
d: one of them is not looking carefully

bank.q: Which sentence describes an object most precisely?
bank.a: a small, badly lit, slightly blurred image
d: a very bad photograph of something
an image that is not very clear
a picture which is quite poor

bank.q: Why does the same shirt look white both at noon and at sunset?
bank.a: the brain removes the colour of the light before reporting the colour of the object
d: the shirt reflects only white light
the eye adjusts its focus automatically

bank.q: A joke that makes you think as well as laugh is …
You could see the ending coming from the first minute; the whole thing was utterly …
The final line of a joke, where the humour lands, is the …
It was not offensive so much as …: the same observation, four times.
You will not understand it … you know the rule it breaks.
Take the subtitles … the sound in that cinema is poor.
Physical comedy travels almost anywhere, … the situation is clear in about five seconds.
A joke can win a worldwide vote … it offends nobody.
In “it works anywhere, as long as the situation is clear”, the phrase as long as introduces …
bank.a: a condition that must stay true

bank.q: Why does a comedy often fail when it crosses a border?
bank.a: the audience does not share the rule the joke breaks

bank.q: A joke wins a global vote by offending nobody. What does that suggest about the vote?
bank.a: it rewards the least objectionable rather than the funniest
d: it was decided by a very small group
the funniest jokes were not entered
the voters had no sense of humour

bank.q: To look at somebody for a fraction of a second and then away again is to …

Which verb suits a deliberate activity followed over time?

bank.a: I happened to see it on the way past.
d: I watched it on the way past.
I stared at it on the way past.
I observed it on the way past.

bank.q: Why do restaurants pay attention to the sound of the room?
bank.a: what people hear changes what they think they taste
d: quiet rooms make people eat faster
music makes food cheaper to produce

Am I right in thinking that?

bank.q: You have understood the words but not the point. Which is the best request?
bank.a: Sorry, I am not sure I follow — what does that mean for us?
d: Sorry, could you repeat all of that?
Sorry, could you speak more slowly?
Sorry, which word was that again?

bank.q: You are describing a photograph and are not certain what you can see. Which is most honest?
bank.a: It looks like a market, though it could be a station.
d: It is a market or something similar, certainly.

bank.q: A brother or a sister is a …

bank.a: returns the reader to what actually happened

bank.q: Why does the writer call sentences like “if I had had a sister” impossible to check?
bank.a: the alternative life was never lived, so there is nothing to compare with
d: families always disagree about the past
the research on the question is incomplete

bank.q: He … the job offer in 2011 and has been explaining it to himself ever since.

bank.a: the first is about now and the second about a finished past

bank.q: “If only I had known” expresses …
Research finds that people regret education more than anything else. The best explanation is that …
bank.a: regret gathers where the door still looks open
d: education matters more than anything else

bank.q: Why does a regret about something not done tend to last longer?
bank.a: there is no single moment to point at, so it never finishes being thought about
d: it is always more serious than a regret about an action

bank.q: Why is vague language common in friendly conversation?
bank.a: precision can sound cold or like showing off
d: speakers rarely know the exact facts

bank.q: Which sentence opens a short biography most effectively?

bank.q: Which sentence reflects on a choice rather than simply reporting it?
bank.a: I took the job for the money, which I would not admit for another decade.
d: I took the job because of the money.
